title: Runbook: Restore Redwood Private to a New Kubernetes Cluster / New VPC
author: Rafael Mendes
body:
## Purpose
This runbook covers **restoring a Redwood Private deployment into a brand-new Kubernetes cluster** (and optionally a brand-new VPC). It is intended for:
- Disaster recovery (original cluster/VPC compromised, unavailable, or unrecoverable).
- Planned migration to new infrastructure (e.g., new region, new VPC design) using a backup as the source of truth.

This runbook focuses on restoring the **control plane first**, validating health, then **cutting over DNS/TLS** and verifying end-to-end API reachability.

> If you are restoring into the **same** cluster (e.g., failed upgrade), use: **Runbook: Restore in-place**.

---

## Ownership / escalation
- Primary on-call owner: **Eng Private Deployments**
- SRE support: **Private SRE (backup/restore SLO owner)**
- Security escalation (keys/certs): **Security Engineering**

Escalate immediately if:
- You do not have access to the backup encryption key material / KMS permissions.
- Restore requires bypassing least-privilege policies (“break-glass”).
- Validation gates fail after multiple attempts and business impact is ongoing.

---

## Definitions
- **Source environment**: the cluster/VPC where the backup was taken.
- **Target environment**: the new cluster/VPC where we restore.
- **Control plane state**: Postgres DB(s), config/policy data, and control-plane-managed object storage data required for the Private API/Console to function.
- **Maintenance mode**: state that blocks control-plane write paths to reduce risk during restore.

---

## Prerequisites (must be true before you start)
### Access and credentials
1. You can authenticate to the target cluster (admin kubeconfig).
2. You can authenticate to the backup repository (S3/GCS/Azure/NFS/minio/local bundle).
3. You have access to backup decryption (KMS/HSM key, or customer-provided key material) and can demonstrate least-privilege.

### Inputs you must have
- Backup identifier (example: `rw-backup-2026-01-07T03-00Z`) and repository URI.
- Redwood Private version to install on the target cluster (must be **compatible** with the backup):
  - Prefer exact same version; otherwise see “Compatibility notes”.
- DNS plan:
  - Whether you will cut over the **same** FQDN (recommended) or introduce a new one.
- TLS plan:
  - Whether you will reuse existing certs (import) or issue new ones.

### Tooling
- `rw-private-dr` CLI available in an operator environment with network reachability to the target cluster and backup repo.
- `kubectl`, `helm` installed.

### Restore window coordination
- Agree on target RTO and who owns cutover:
  - Solutions lead (customer comms), SRE (timeline + evidence), Eng Private (technical execution).

---

## Safety notes (read before executing)
- Restoring to a new cluster is **destructive** to the target environment state. Use a fresh cluster or ensure no production state exists.
- If you plan to reuse the same DNS name, ensure the old environment is:
  - Down / isolated from clients, or
  - Put into a state where it cannot accept writes (to avoid split-brain / diverging state).
- Do not log secrets. Redact KMS key IDs, access tokens, and cert material in tickets and shared channels.

---

## High-level workflow
1. **Provision target infrastructure** (VPC/networking/storage/IAM/KMS).
2. **Bootstrap target cluster** (base dependencies + Redwood Private baseline install).
3. **Plan restore** (validate backup, validate target readiness).
4. **Restore control plane DB(s)** (PITR if required).
5. **Restore artifacts/config** (object storage snapshots; secrets/certs per policy).
6. **Bring services up in correct order** and run validation gates.
7. **Cut over DNS/TLS** and verify external reachability.
8. **Post-cutover checks** + evidence capture.

---

## Compatibility notes (version + schema)
- Backups are expected to be compatible with the same Redwood Private minor release line.
- If restoring across versions:
  - Prefer: restore at the same version as the backup, then perform a standard upgrade.
  - If you must restore onto a newer version, you must confirm DB migration compatibility with Eng Private.
- If `rw-private-dr restore plan` reports migration risk, stop and escalate.

---

## Step 0 — Evidence capture (do this at the beginning)
Create an evidence folder (ticket attachment or internal doc) with:
- Operator names and roles
- Start timestamp
- Target cluster name/region/VPC ID
- Backup ID + repository URI
- KMS key reference (redacted) and IAM role used
- Planned DNS cutover approach

Recommended template fields:
- `restore_run_id` (example: `restore-2026-01-10-001`)
- `backup_id`
- `target_cluster_context`
- `operator_bastion_host`

---

## Step 1 — Provision target infrastructure (VPC + storage + IAM)
> If you are restoring to a new cluster **within an existing VPC**, still confirm endpoint access (S3 gateway / PrivateLink, etc.).

### 1.1 Networking checks
Confirm the target cluster has network access to:
- Backup repository endpoint (S3/GCS/Azure/minio/NFS)
- KMS/HSM endpoint (if applicable)
- Internal dependencies used by the Private control plane (as per customer deployment)

Validation commands (examples):
- `kubectl -n redwood-private exec -it deploy/rw-ops-toolbox -- curl -I https://s3.<region>.amazonaws.com`
- `kubectl -n redwood-private exec -it deploy/rw-ops-toolbox -- nslookup <backup-endpoint>`

### 1.2 Create/verify storage targets
Ensure:
- Backup repository exists and is accessible from target cluster.
- Restore writes (if required) are permitted (some flows require temporary staging).

### 1.3 IAM / KMS wiring
- Use least-privilege role policies.
- If using a “break-glass” role, ensure approvals are recorded.

---

## Step 2 — Bootstrap the target cluster (baseline install)
The goal is to install the **minimum** Redwood Private footprint required to run restore jobs and then bring control plane up safely.

### 2.1 Install prerequisites
- Namespaces
- CSI drivers / storage class
- Ingress / load balancer controller (per customer)
- ExternalDNS (if used)
- Secrets store CSI driver (if used)

### 2.2 Install Redwood Private baseline
Install Redwood Private using the customer-approved method (installer/Helm/Terraform wrappers).

Required: set **maintenance mode ON** for restore bootstrap.
- This prevents writes during DB replay and control-plane stabilization.

Example (conceptual; actual values depend on chart/installer):
- `helm upgrade --install redwood-private redwood/private \
  -n redwood-private \
  -f values.yaml \
  --set maintenanceMode.enabled=true`

Confirm maintenance mode is active:
- `kubectl -n redwood-private get configmap rw-maintenance-mode -o yaml`
- OR via API once reachable internally (later step).

### 2.3 Confirm pods for restore tooling are ready
- `kubectl -n redwood-private get pods`

You should have:
- Postgres (or external DB connectivity) available for restore
- Ops/restore job runner image pull succeeds

If image pulls fail due to private registry access, stop and fix registry credentials.

---

## Step 3 — Plan the restore (preflight + gating)
### 3.1 Fetch backup metadata and validate integrity
Run from your operator environment:
- `rw-private-dr backup verify \
  --repo <REPO_URI> \
  --backup-id <BACKUP_ID> \
  --verify-checksums \
  --verify-encryption`

Expected output (example):
- `OK checksums: manifest.sha256 verified`
- `OK encryption: envelope key via KMS`
- `OK contents: control-plane-db, object-artifacts, config-policies`

If verification fails:
- Do not proceed.
- See SRE troubleshooting page for common failure modes (AccessDenied, partial uploads, checksum mismatch).

### 3.2 Plan restore against target cluster
- `rw-private-dr restore plan \
  --kube-context <TARGET_CONTEXT> \
  --repo <REPO_URI> \
  --backup-id <BACKUP_ID> \
  --restore-mode new-cluster \
  --output plan.json`

Plan should report:
- Target version compatibility
- Which components will be restored
- Required secrets/certs inputs (if any)
- Estimated time (best-effort)

Stop conditions:
- Plan includes “manual intervention required” for DB schema mismatch.
- Plan cannot detect/validate DB endpoint.

---

## Step 4 — Restore the control plane DB(s) (first)
This step differs depending on whether Postgres is:
- Managed externally (RDS/Cloud SQL/Azure Database), or
- In-cluster.

### 4.1 Ensure writes are blocked
Confirm maintenance mode is ON (again). If you need to keep some read-only endpoints available internally, confirm with Eng Private.

### 4.2 Execute DB restore
#### Option A: Full restore from dump
- `rw-private-dr restore execute \
  --kube-context <TARGET_CONTEXT> \
  --repo <REPO_URI> \
  --backup-id <BACKUP_ID> \
  --components postgres \
  --strategy full \
  --wait`

#### Option B: PITR (Point-in-time restore)
Use PITR only if:
- WAL archiving was configured at backup time, and
- You have an approved target timestamp.

- `rw-private-dr restore execute \
  --kube-context <TARGET_CONTEXT> \
  --repo <REPO_URI> \
  --backup-id <BACKUP_ID> \
  --components postgres \
  --strategy pitr \
  --pitr-target "2026-01-07T02:57:00Z" \
  --wait`

### 4.3 Validate DB health
Examples:
- `kubectl -n redwood-private logs job/rw-restore-postgres -f`
- `kubectl -n redwood-private exec -it deploy/rw-ops-toolbox -- psql "$RW_DATABASE_URL" -c 'select 1;'`

Acceptance criteria:
- DB is reachable
- Restore job exits 0
- No repeated migration errors in logs

---

## Step 5 — Restore object artifacts + config/policy data
### 5.1 Restore object artifacts
These typically include:
- Model/catalog artifacts used by the control plane
- Cached metadata needed for startup
- Selected logs/exports if configured

- `rw-private-dr restore execute \
  --kube-context <TARGET_CONTEXT> \
  --repo <REPO_URI> \
  --backup-id <BACKUP_ID> \
  --components object-artifacts,config \
  --wait`

### 5.2 Secrets and certificates
Follow customer policy:
- **Preferred**: secrets are sourced from customer secret manager (not restored from backup).
- If the backup includes encrypted secret bundles (allowed only in certain customer profiles), confirm:
  - encryption keys are customer-owned
  - restore is approved by Security + customer operator

TLS options:
1. **Reuse existing certs** (same FQDN): import cert+key into target secret store.
2. **Issue new certs**: update FQDN or re-issue via customer CA.

Hard requirement:
- The **API endpoint FQDN** you intend to cut over must have a matching TLS certificate ready **before** DNS cutover.

---

## Step 6 — Bring up control plane services (sequencing)
After DB + artifacts are restored:
1. Start/verify core control plane services (config/policy services first).
2. Start API gateway / ingress.
3. Start console (if deployed).

Typical sequence (may vary by install):
1. `rw-config`
2. `rw-policy`
3. `rw-control-plane-api`
4. `rw-console`

Commands:
- `kubectl -n redwood-private rollout status deploy/rw-config --timeout=10m`
- `kubectl -n redwood-private rollout status deploy/rw-control-plane-api --timeout=10m`

If pods crashloop:
- Check DB connectivity, secrets mounts, and configmaps first.

---

## Step 7 — Validation gates (internal)
Do not cut over DNS until validation gates pass.

### 7.1 Health checks
From inside the VPC or via bastion:
- `curl -sf https://<INTERNAL_API_ENDPOINT>/healthz`
- `curl -sf https://<INTERNAL_API_ENDPOINT>/readyz`

Expected:
- `200 OK` for health/ready.

### 7.2 Smoke tests (API)
Run the restore validation gate if available:
- `rw-private-dr restore validate \
  --kube-context <TARGET_CONTEXT> \
  --api-endpoint https://<INTERNAL_API_ENDPOINT> \
  --timeout 10m`

If you don’t have `restore validate` in your version, run manual checks:
- Auth token mint (if applicable)
- List models (control plane): `GET /v1/models` (or customer equivalent)
- Create a small non-destructive resource if permitted (otherwise read-only checks)

### 7.3 Observability checks
Confirm metrics/log shipping is functioning for the target cluster:
- Backup/restore dashboard shows a restore event/annotation (if configured)
- Control plane logs flowing to expected sink (customer SIEM/export)

---

## Step 8 — Cutover (DNS + TLS)
### 8.1 Decide cutover method
Common options:
- **DNS cutover** (recommended): lower TTL, then update A/AAAA/CNAME to new load balancer.
- **LB swap**: depends on customer infrastructure; ensure cert attachment and security groups are correct.

### 8.2 Pre-cutover checklist
- [ ] Target cluster validation gates passed
- [ ] TLS certificate active on target ingress
- [ ] Firewall/Security Groups allow required client traffic
- [ ] Old environment is prevented from accepting writes (or is offline)
- [ ] DNS TTL lowered (e.g., 60s) for at least one TTL interval before change

### 8.3 Execute DNS change
Update the authoritative record(s) for the production FQDN.

Capture evidence:
- Before/after DNS values
- Timestamp of record update
- TTL value

### 8.4 Validate external reachability
From a client network that mirrors production access:
- `curl -sv https://<PROD_FQDN>/healthz`
- Run a minimal “known-good” API call used by customer monitors

If clients see TLS errors:
- Confirm cert SAN matches FQDN
- Confirm intermediate chain
- Confirm ingress is serving the correct secret

---

## Step 9 — Disable maintenance mode (only after cutover validation)
Once you are confident the restored environment is serving correctly:
- Disable maintenance mode.

Example (conceptual):
- `helm upgrade redwood-private redwood/private -n redwood-private --reuse-values --set maintenanceMode.enabled=false`

Validate:
- Previously blocked write endpoints return normal responses
- Control plane error rate returns to baseline

---

## Step 10 — Post-cutover checks (15–60 minutes)
Monitor:
- API 5xx rate
- Latency (p50/p95)
- Auth/token failures
- DB CPU / connections
- Control plane queue/backlog (if applicable)

Confirm scheduled backups are configured on the new environment:
- CronJob exists and is not suspended
- Next run window is acceptable

Commands:
- `kubectl -n redwood-private get cronjob | grep backup`
- `kubectl -n redwood-private describe cronjob rw-backup`

---

## Rollback plan (if cutover fails)
Rollback choices depend on what is broken:
1. **DNS rollback**: point DNS back to old environment (fastest).
2. **Keep DNS on new, re-enable maintenance mode**, fix issues, then disable.

Guidance:
- If the new environment returns errors that will not be fixed quickly, prefer DNS rollback.
- If the issue is limited (e.g., missing integration secret) and can be corrected quickly, keep DNS and fix.

Always capture:
- Reason for rollback
- Timestamps
- Evidence (error logs, failed checks)

---

## Common failure modes (quick triage)
### AccessDenied to backup repo
Symptoms:
- Restore jobs fail with `AccessDenied` / `403`.

Actions:
- Validate IAM role binding used by restore job (IRSA/workload identity).
- Validate bucket policy/KMS policy allows decrypt.

### Checksum mismatch / partial uploads
Symptoms:
- `backup verify` fails checksums.

Actions:
- Do not proceed.
- Locate prior “last known good” backup snapshot.
- Investigate storage throttling / multipart upload issues.

### Restore takes longer than window
Symptoms:
- DB restore or artifact restore exceeds expected.

Actions:
- Confirm resource requests/limits for restore job runner.
- Confirm backend throttling (S3 request rate, minio perf).
- For DB: check locks, IO throughput, and restore strategy.

### TLS errors after cutover
Symptoms:
- `x509: certificate is valid for ...`

Actions:
- Confirm secret referenced by ingress
- Confirm cert SAN includes FQDN
- Confirm chain is complete

---

## Appendix A — Minimal command summary
Replace placeholders before running.

1) Verify backup
- `rw-private-dr backup verify --repo <REPO_URI> --backup-id <BACKUP_ID> --verify-checksums --verify-encryption`

2) Plan restore
- `rw-private-dr restore plan --kube-context <TARGET_CONTEXT> --repo <REPO_URI> --backup-id <BACKUP_ID> --restore-mode new-cluster --output plan.json`

3) Execute restore (DB then artifacts)
- `rw-private-dr restore execute --kube-context <TARGET_CONTEXT> --repo <REPO_URI> --backup-id <BACKUP_ID> --components postgres --strategy full --wait`
- `rw-private-dr restore execute --kube-context <TARGET_CONTEXT> --repo <REPO_URI> --backup-id <BACKUP_ID> --components object-artifacts,config --wait`

4) Validate
- `curl -sf https://<INTERNAL_API_ENDPOINT>/healthz`
- `rw-private-dr restore validate --kube-context <TARGET_CONTEXT> --api-endpoint https://<INTERNAL_API_ENDPOINT> --timeout 10m`

5) Cutover
- Update DNS for `<PROD_FQDN>` to new LB
- Validate: `curl -sv https://<PROD_FQDN>/healthz`

---

## Appendix B — Cutover checklist (copy/paste)
- [ ] Evidence doc created (restore_run_id, timestamps, operators)
- [ ] Target infra provisioned (network endpoints, IAM/KMS)
- [ ] Target baseline installed with maintenance mode enabled
- [ ] Backup verified (checksums + encryption)
- [ ] Restore plan reviewed; no blocking incompatibilities
- [ ] Control plane DB restore completed successfully
- [ ] Artifact/config restore completed successfully
- [ ] Core services rolled out; pods healthy
- [ ] Internal health/ready endpoints OK
- [ ] Smoke tests OK
- [ ] TLS certificate ready and attached on target ingress
- [ ] Old environment write paths blocked or offline
- [ ] DNS TTL lowered
- [ ] DNS updated to target LB
- [ ] External reachability verified
- [ ] Maintenance mode disabled
- [ ] Post-cutover monitoring stable (15–60 min)
- [ ] Backups scheduled and verified on new environment

---

## Change log
- 2026-01-10: Updated validation section to include `rw-private-dr restore validate` and clarified TLS prerequisites before DNS cutover.
- 2025-11-22: Initial published runbook for new-cluster restore flow.
